thread.title_full: As Rays shop for help, Ryan Vilade delivers again in win over Rangers - NewsBreak

author: Tampa Bay Times
title: As Rays shop for help, Ryan Vilade delivers again in win over Rangers - NewsBreak
text:
2 hours ago The Rays' Ryan Vilade pumps a fist as he rounds the bases on a second-inning home run Wednesday night against the Rangers. [ LUIS SANTANA | Times ] If you believe what you read, hear and scroll through on social media, the Rays’ shopping list ahead of Monday’s trade deadline includes acquiring a hitter, likely an outfielder, who can add some power, production and presence behind the big three at the top of their order.
As they evaluate potential options, weigh the acquisition cost in prospects or big-league pieces and consider how a new addition might fit in their closely-knit clubhouse, Ryan Vilade just keeps showing how much he can do to help.
Wednesday, Vilade hit a two-run homer in the first inning to help lead to the Rays to a 3-0 victory over the American League West-leading Rangers.
“He’s coming up big for us,” manager Kevin Cash said. “He fits our team really, really well, and he’s played a huge role. Whether he’s in there every day or not, he’s always ready. And when he gets his opportunities, he’s just come up with so many big hits, big home runs here this season.”
Talk about a slump buster. Yandy Diaz hits a home run in the first inning. [ LUIS SANTANA | Times ] Yandy Diaz also homered to lead off the home first, and five pitchers — Casey Legumina, Ian Seymour, Garrett Cleavinger, Kevin Kelly and Bryan Baker — combined for the Rays’ third shutout in their last four games and ninth overall.
The Rays improved their AL-best record to 63-44 (a season high-matching 19 games over .500) and, at the least, maintained their 1 ½-game East division lead over the Yankees, who were playing late at Chicago.
Vilade in a limited role — 59 games (42 starts) and 159 at-bats — has had a big part, posting nine homers (fifth most on the team), 35 RBIs (fourth most) and an .804 OPS (fourth most), while starting at four positions. Wednesday’s blast, estimated at 420 feet as it struck either the D-ring catwalk or the attached light post, was his sixth to carry at least 400.
The Rays were the first team to give Vilade, 27, much of a chance, acquiring him in a November cash trade. Before that he’d played in 28 big-league games total over parts of three seasons with the Rockies, Tigers, Cardinals and Reds.
“Just your typical Tampa Bay surprise,” said Diaz, via team interpreter Kevin Vera. “He’s gotten some playing time, and when he has gotten the playing time, he’s capitalized on it. So credit to him.”
Seymour is also a fan.
“It speaks to the character of him to always be ready, and it just gives us so much energy on the bench at all times because he’s constantly engaged,” he said. “Couldn’t be happier to see him hit a ball out of the yard there.”
Ryan Vilade is making the most of his consistent playing time with the Rays. “It’s been good that they trust me to go out there and play, and I trust them." [ LUIS SANTANA | Times ] Vilade, a right-handed hitter who gets most of his starts against lefty pitchers, said he greatly appreciates the opportunity the Rays have provided.
“It’s been good that they trust me to go out there and play, and I trust them,” he said. “I know they’re going to put me in spots to go out there and be successful. It’s been a great year, and we’re going to just keep it rolling.”
The Rays overall are trying to do the same, seeking to get back to the playoffs for the first time since 2023 and to advance for the first time since their 2020 COVID-season World Series run, having lost their last seven playoff games over 2021-22-23.
The dominant pitching they’ve shown lately is certainly a good sign, just the fourth time in 29 seasons they have posted three shutouts in a four-game stretch.
“I feel like our starters over the course of the season have done a really good job,” Cash said. “I know they’re on a good run right now, but they’re pitching with a lot of confidence. And I think anytime they go on runs like that, there’s a little bit of competition amongst the group. A lot of respect, but competition. They want to go out and (out)do each other.”
Added Diaz: “There’s not much you can say, really. The only thing that comes to mind is ... our pitchers are nasty. They’ve been doing their job the entire time. So it’s really good to have them."
Rays pitcher Ian Seymour enters the game in the second inning behind the opener, then pitches into the seventh. [ LUIS SANTANA | Times ] Legumina retired the first five Rangers, then was lifted after allowing a two-out double in the second. It was the ninth-straight game a Tampa Bay starter allowed two or fewer runs.
Seymour took over and worked effectively and efficiently into the seventh. Cleavinger got the Rays out of a two-on, one-out jam. Kelly handled the eighth and Baker the ninth for his 29th save, having converted his last 18 opportunities.
“Not surprising,” Baker said. “It’s fun to watch them go out there and do their thing. (The five pitchers) ) were nails tonight. It’s fun to play defense behind them.”
Diaz had been in a bit of a slump, coming into play Wednesday 2-for-his-last-15.
Cash said before the game Diaz was “just not timed up right now,” getting caught “a little in-between” on some pitches and missing some others he usually hits square, but “it can take one swing or one at-bat to get him right.”
Diaz said the opposite-field homer — the first for the Rays after three games without anyone going deep — was a good sign.
“I’m just trying to find my rhythm the entire time and find my timing,” he said. “(Wednesday) it just kind of worked out.”
Baker, who pitched parts of five seasons in the majors before getting his first closing opportunity with the Rays this season, can relate to Vilade’s journey.
“I know where he’s been,” Baker said. “It’s hard to get opportunities in this league and if you don’t perform well, sometimes you don’t get any more. So just seeing him kind of embrace this role and the way the team really respects him and loves his presence in this clubhouse is pretty cool, too, which I think is even bigger than what he’s doing on the field. And what he’s doing on the field is pretty darn good, too.
“So, yeah, I’d say we’re pretty lucky to have him, and it’s a great story, man. It shows that you stick with something and persevere and take advantage of your opportunities, good things can happen.”
